answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**A district court abuses its discretion when it denies transfer to a clearly more convenient venue.**

Section 1404(a) authorizes transfer "[f]or the convenience of parties and witnesses, in the interest of justice." 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a). The statute commits that decision to the district court's discretion, but discretion is bounded by governing legal standards. "A district court by definition abuses its discretion when it makes an error of law." *Moore v. Ashland Chem. Inc.*, 151 F.3d 269, 274 (5th Cir. 1998) (en banc) (quoting *Koon v. United States*, 518 U.S. 81, 100 (1996)). The same is true when a court relies on clearly erroneous factual findings or misapplies the law to the facts. *McClure v. Ashcroft*, 335 F.3d 404, 408 (5th Cir. 2003); *see In re Volkswagen of Am., Inc.*, 545 F.3d 304, 310 (5th Cir. 2008) (en banc).

The en banc Court has stated the governing rule. A movant must show good cause for transfer, which respects the plaintiff's initial choice of forum. *Volkswagen*, 545 F.3d at 315. That choice prevails when the proposed venue is not clearly more convenient. *Id.* But "[w]hen the movant demonstrates that the transferee venue is clearly more convenient, . . . it has shown good cause and the district court should therefore grant the transfer." *Id.* The plaintiff's choice thus determines the movant's burden. It is not an independent reason to deny transfer once that burden has been carried. *See id.* at 314–15 & n.10.

Whether the burden has been met turns on established criteria. After asking whether the suit could have been brought in the proposed district, the court weighs private-interest factors: relative ease of access to sources of proof; availability of compulsory process; cost of attendance for willing witnesses; and other practical problems affecting an easy, expeditious, and inexpensive trial. *In re Volkswagen AG*, 371 F.3d 201, 203 (5th Cir. 2004). It also weighs public-interest factors: court congestion; the local interest in deciding localized disputes at home; the forum's familiarity with the governing law; and the avoidance of unnecessary conflicts of law. *Id.* No single factor is dispositive. *Action Indus., Inc. v. U.S. Fid. & Guar. Co.*, 358 F.3d 337, 340 (5th Cir. 2004). Flexibility in weighing these factors does not permit a court to disregard them, distort them, or substitute considerations that this Court has rejected.

This Court has repeatedly enforced those limits, even under the demanding mandamus standard, which requires a clear abuse of discretion producing a patently erroneous result. *Volkswagen*, 545 F.3d at 310–12. In *Volkswagen*, the district court gave undue weight to the plaintiffs' choice of venue and misapplied the convenience factors, although the evidence, witnesses, and events were centered in the proposed forum. *Id.* at 315–18. The en banc Court held that those errors warranted mandamus. *Id.* at 318–19. A panel had likewise granted mandamus in *Volkswagen AG*, where the district court failed to properly consider the convenience of the parties and witnesses and the public interest. 371 F.3d at 203–06.

The principle applies with equal force to other recurring errors. Witness inconvenience increases with the additional distance witnesses must travel when the two venues are more than 100 miles apart. *Id.* at 204–05; *Volkswagen*, 545 F.3d at 317. A court may not discount that burden merely because modern transportation makes travel possible, or because documents can be moved electronically. *See Volkswagen*, 545 F.3d at 316–17; *In re Radmax, Ltd.*, 720 F.3d 285, 288–89 (5th Cir. 2013). Nor may it treat a generalized interest in the chosen forum as equivalent to the concrete interest of the locality where the events occurred. *Volkswagen*, 545 F.3d at 317–18. *Radmax* granted mandamus and required transfer where the district court's errors in assessing the factors led it to retain a case that belonged in a clearly more convenient division. 720 F.3d at 288–90; *see also In re Horseshoe Ent.*, 337 F.3d 429, 433–35 (5th Cir. 2003) (granting mandamus to require transfer).

Accordingly, once the record establishes that the transferee venue is clearly more convenient, denial is not a permissible choice among reasonable alternatives. It rests on a misapplication of § 1404(a). Because Defendant has made that showing, the denial of transfer was an abuse of discretion and should be reversed, with instructions to transfer.
